question: Two guitar strings almost in tune make a slow wah-wah-wah. What is that wobble counting?
answer: The gap between their frequencies. Two waves a few cycles apart drift in and out of step: where peaks meet the sound swells, where they cancel it dips. Strings at 55 and 58 Hz swell 3 times a second. Players turn the peg until the wobble slows to nothing; piano tuners count it.
move: To match two things closely, watch their mismatch, not either one.
ask: Where could I spot a small difference by watching two things drift apart?

scene.hint: Tap two keys a step apart, low down, and listen for the wobble.

moments.name: 3 swells a second
moments.text: 55 and 58.3 Hz, heard as one note swelling 3 times a second: the gap.

moments.name: 6.5 a second
moments.text: The same step an octave up, 110 and 116.5 Hz: twice the gap, twice the wobble.

moments.name: No wobble
moments.text: An octave, 1 : 2. The high wave fits the low one exactly; nothing drifts.

moments.name: One every 5 s
moments.text: A piano's fifth: harmonics at 165 and 164.8 Hz swell once every 5 seconds.

source: Rossing et al., The Science of Sound, 2002
reference: Rossing, Moore & Wheeler, The Science of Sound, 3rd edn, Addison-Wesley, 2002, ch. 8 (beats: the beat rate is the difference of the two frequencies); equal-tempered A1 55 Hz, Bb1 58.27 Hz, E2 82.41 Hz
